## Claims — grouped by pericope

### 4:1–6 (Christian Unity and Its Theological Basis)

- **[4:1]** The οὖν (oun, therefore) reaches back to all of chs. 1–3 but particularly the church-unity theme; marks the theology-to-ethics turn typical of Paul. Thielman: "This movement from theology to ethics... is a common feature of the Pauline Letters" (parallels 1 Cor 4:15–16; Rom 12:1). *Thielman.*
- **[4:1]** παρακαλῶ signals ethical advice given "in the context of friendship" — Thielman grounds this in the near-contemporary letter to Philemon (Philem. 8–10), "written at virtually the same time as Ephesians." *Thielman* (dating claim: attributed to Thielman).
- **[4:1]** "the prisoner in the Lord" recalls 3:1, 3:13; gives "a certain gravitas" — Paul willing "to suffer the physical pain and social stigma of imprisonment." *Thielman.*
- **[4:1]** περιπατέω (peripatēsai, walk) picks up 2:1–10; the "calling" (κλήσεως... ἐκλήθητε) refers to conversion and, per 1:18 and 4:4, is "oriented primarily toward the believer's future 'hope.'" *Thielman.*
- **[4:2–3]** Four expressions are adverbial modifiers of περιπατῆσαι; the two nominative participles (ἀνεχόμενοι, σπουδάζοντες) most commentators read as imperatival (Best, O'Brien, Hoehner), but Thielman follows Abbott/Wallace: they "agree with the logical subject of περιπατῆσαι." Robinson: "St Paul is fond of passing suddenly to the nominative of a participle." *Thielman siding with Abbott/Wallace/Robinson vs. Best/O'Brien/Hoehner.*
- **[4:2]** ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosynē, humility) "is uncommon in first-century Greek, but when it occurs, it has decidedly negative connotations" — Josephus on Galba (J.W. 4.494), Epictetus (opposite of γενναῖος gennaios "noble spirit"), ridiculed by Origen (Cels. 6.15). Positive Christian sense "came from the Jewish Scriptures." *Thielman.*
- **[4:2]** πραΰτης (praytēs) = "gentleness"/"politeness" esp. when effort is required. Together the terms denote recognizing one's "true position before God (a suppliant in need of his help)" while being kind under provocation. *Thielman (BDAG-based).*
- **[4:2]** μακροθυμία (makrothymia, patience) = "persistence in one's convictions... 'being able to bear up under provocation.'" ἀνέχω (anechō) = put up with the annoying/harmful, but "in love" excludes grudging tolerance (cf. Col 3:13). *Thielman.*
- **[4:3]** σπουδάζοντες τηρεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ πνεύματος — the climactic phrase and bridge to vv. 4–6. ἑνότης (henotēs, unity/oneness) "points ahead"; "one" appears six times in 34 words in vv. 4–6. *Thielman.*
- **[4:3]** Unity is "complex": already possessed via the Spirit (2:18, 22) yet must be maintained (τηρεῖν) and lived zealously. σύνδεσμος (syndesmos) = "fastener" (clothing clasp, grammatical conjunction, or ligament); in Stoicism/Middle Platonism the bond holding "the cosmic body of the universe together" (van Kooten). "peace is the 'fastener' that preserves the church's unity." *Thielman.*
- **[4:4–6]** The seven "ones" (body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God-Father) — seven being "a significant number in Judaism and early Christianity." Features (no main verb, no linking conjunction, threefold gender play in v.5) lead many to see an "early Christian creedal formulation," whole (Pelikan & Hotchkiss) or part (Lincoln, Best). *Reported positions.*
- **[4:4–6]** Thielman's own view: "it seems likely... that Paul freely composed 4:4–6 as he dictated his letter, perhaps relying to some extent on traditional language from early creedal formulations" — analogy to 1 Cor 8:4, so integrated that source-elements are hard to isolate. *Thielman.*
- **[4:4]** ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα reaches back to 2:13–22 (Christ as peace, one new human being, one body via the cross). *Thielman.*
- **[4:4]** "one hope" (ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι) — hope "accompanied God's call, as an integral part of it"; likened to Abraham's trust (Rom 4:17–18) in the unseen. *Thielman.*
- **[4:5]** εἷς κύριος, μία πίστις, ἓν βάπτισμα — the three genders show "his emphasis lies on the numeral itself and not on the three terms"; cautions against reading significance into their order/selection. *Thielman.*
- **[4:5]** "one Lord" excludes imperial claims — Nero inscription "ὁ τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου κύριος Νέρων" (SIG 814); and identifies Jesus with the LXX κύριος of Deut 6:4 ("κύριος εἷς"). *Thielman.*
- **[4:5]** "one faith" — could be body of doctrine (Best, O'Brien) or trust in Christ (Eadie, Hoehner). Thielman: "Paul probably means the body of teaching that Christians believe" (drawing on 4:13 ἡ ἑνότης τῆς πίστεως = content handed on by the 4:11 leaders). *Thielman siding with Best/O'Brien.*
- **[4:5]** "one baptism" — most read water immersion (BDAG), but βαπτίζω means "I immerse," not "I immerse in water." Rich echoes of 1 Cor 12:13 → Spirit-immersion primary; Gal 3:26–29 baptism read metaphorically (Dunn). Thielman's conclusion: "best to think of 'one baptism' as a shorthand expression for the whole process of conversion, summarized by reference to the visible ritual" — the ritual important but "not nearly as important as the spiritual reality." *Thielman, heavily via Dunn.*
- **[4:6]** Climactic seventh "one." Fourfold "all" (πάντων...πᾶσιν) — masculine (= all believers: Alford, Eadie, Bruce, Schnackenburg, Hoehner) or neuter (= all things: Gnilka, Barth, O'Brien, Lincoln, Darko). Thielman: those reading neuter "have the better argument" — Pauline parallels 1 Cor 8:6, Rom 11:36, Col 1:16–17, plus Ephesians' "all things" theme (1:10, 11, 22; 3:9, 15). *Thielman siding with neuter reading.*
- **[4:6]** God "over all" = creator/subjector of all to Christ; "through/in all" = summing up all in Christ. Parallels Stoic omnipresence language (Marcus Aurelius; noted since Jerome) and Hellenistic Jewish "one Father of all" (Josephus Ag. Ap. 2.193; Philo Spec. Laws 1.14). *Thielman.*
- **[4:6 Additional Note]** Textual variant ἡμῖν ("in us all") after ἐν πᾶσιν — witnesses D, F, G, Ψ, Byz, OL, Syr, Irenaeus. If original, decides the masc/neut question for masculine (believers); Hoehner accepts it. But most commentators omit (Ellicott, Abbott, Robinson, Lincoln, Best, Metzger); strong early witnesses against (𝔓46, א, A, B, C...). Origen/Marcion debated whether God is Father of all or only Christians — motive for a scribe adding ἡμῖν. Thielman: "It is likely, then, that ἡμῖν was not part of the original letter." *Thielman.*

### 4:7–10 (the gift-giver, victorious Christ)

- **[4:7]** ἑνὶ δὲ ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν — "one" links to unity theme; grace "given to each believer κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ (according to the measure of the gift of Christ)." χάρις carries not just an assignment but "the gift of 'the powers and capabilities requisite' to complete the assignment" (BDAG). *Thielman.*
- **[4:7]** Minority view (Merklein 1973) that "us" = only the office-holders of v.11, from a post-Pauline author sanctioning ecclesiastical offices. Thielman rejects: "not a plausible reading" — the first-person plural throughout the letter includes writer with readers (Schnackenburg). *Thielman vs. Merklein.*
- **[4:8]** Introductory διὸ λέγει (dio legei, therefore it says) — appears only here, 5:14, James 4:6 in NT; unusually does not name its source. Quotation resembles Ps 68:18 (68:19 MT; 67:19 LXX) but differs importantly. *Thielman.*
- **[4:8]** Three changes vs. MT/LXX (which agree): (1) 2nd person → 3rd person (God → Christ); (2) collective singular "humanity" → plural "human beings"; (3) most important, verb "received" (ἔλαβες) → its antonym "gave" (ἔδωκεν). Original Ps 68:18 = God taking booty from defeated enemies on a mountaintop; Paul = "triumphant Christ distributing gifts to each of his human subjects." *Thielman (primary-text comparison).*
- **[4:8]** The Jewish interpretive tradition (Midr. Teh., Targum on Ps 68:19) read the psalm of Moses' ascent to heaven to receive Torah; the Targum actually substitutes "he gave" for "you received" ("you gave them as gifts to the sons of men"). W. H. Harris 1996 central here. Some think Paul knew this tradition; others (Lincoln, Bruce) that Paul used it polemically (Moses gave law, Christ gave grace; Moses ascended to heaven, Christ "far above the heavens"); a variant sees an early Christian anti-Moses/Pentecost argument (Harris, Schnackenburg, Moritz, Muddiman). *Reported positions.*
- **[4:8]** Thielman's own conclusion: "the balance of the evidence favors the view that Paul himself changed the text of the psalm." Two grounds: (1) only the Targum (4th–5th c.) unambiguously has "gave," and it may be a polemical response to Christian exegesis (which predates it — Justin, Tertullian); (2) Paul "wrote in Greek to Gentiles in Asia Minor," would not assume familiarity with an Aramaic paraphrase. Parallels Paul's free citation elsewhere (Hab 2:4 in Gal 3:11/Rom 1:17; Deut 30:12–14 in Rom 10:6–8). Paul's change is nonetheless "consistent with the overall theological direction of Ps 68" (a psalm of God's military triumph, vv. 17–18 being its climax). *Thielman.*

### The descent (4:9) — full detail (see dedicated section below)

- **[4:10]** Two assertions: (1) descender and ascender are "identical" — Thielman: NOT to make a christological point about incarnate-vs-heavenly Christ (pace Jerome, Theodoret, Eadie) nor a pneumatological point (pace W. H. Harris), but to prepare v.11: "the very one who both descended and ascended is the one who gave gifts." The emphatic αὐτός (4:10) is repeated in 4:11. *Thielman.*
- **[4:10]** (2) Purpose: he ascended "far above the heavens" so that "like God himself in verse 6, he might fill all things" (Aletti). Picture parallels 1:20–23; Christ's victory is "not merely for himself but also for the church, which as his body joins him in filling every corner of the universe (1:23)." *Thielman.*

### 4:11–13 (the gifts and their goal)

- **[4:11]** αὐτός (he himself) gave gifts to "discrete groups of people" who in turn equip others. "the most plausible understanding... places the emphasis less on the positions that certain people hold... and more on the activities that Christ has equipped certain people to perform." Five groups. *Thielman.*
- **[4:11]** Apostles (ἀποστόλους) — with prophets "the foundation" (2:20); always listed first; place of "greatest foundational importance because of their connection with the historical Jesus" (cf. 3:5). Paul counts himself least/last (1 Cor 15:8–9). *Thielman.*
- **[4:11]** Prophets (προφήτας) — "not OT prophets but people living in Paul's own time" prompted by the Spirit; reveal "mysteries," notably Gentile inclusion (3:5–6); placed second because of that role. *Thielman.*
- **[4:11]** Evangelists (εὐαγγελιστάς) — of Christian coinage; the term's cognates "involve the element of traveling," so evangelists are "those whom God has especially equipped to travel from place to place with the good news of peace through Christ." Like apostles but without their authority "because of their lack of direct connection to the historical Jesus" (Friedrich). *Thielman.*
- **[4:11]** Pastors-and-teachers (τοὺς δὲ ποιμένας καὶ διδασκάλους) — grouped under a single τοὺς δέ, joined by καί. See dedicated one-or-two-office section below. ποιμήν = "shepherd," metaphor for political/religious leader; OT God-as-shepherd, David, future David (Ezek 34); 1 Pet 5:1–4 connects it with "elders." In 4:11 shepherds were "leaders within Christian communities who held positions of authority," esp. concerned to protect the flock from "savage wolves" of false teaching (Acts 20:28–30; cf. Eph 4:14). *Thielman.*
- **[4:11]** Teachers (διδασκάλους) — though "the first four groups... will all have been teachers," there was a specialized group (1 Thess 5:12; 1 Cor 12:28; Rom 12:7); they instruct in "the teaching" (ἡ διδασκαλία), which in Ephesians is to "learn Christ" (4:20). Given the 4:14 false-teaching concern, teachers play "a particularly critical role." *Thielman.*
- **[4:12]** Three prepositional phrases; debate over the middle εἰς ἔργον διακονίας (for the work of ministry). **View 1** (coordinate): all three phrases modify ἔδωκεν; the five groups themselves do the ministry. Ancient (Chrysostom, John of Damascus, Calvin), "exegetically well supported," fits Ephesians' style of stacked prepositional phrases (1:3; 1:5–6), and best fits διακονία as "ministry of the word" with official nuance. *Reported (View 1).*
- **[4:12]** **View 2** (dependent): εἰς ἔργον διακονίας fills out καταρτισμόν; the five groups "prepare or equip the saints 'for the work of ministry.'" Thielman's own conclusion: "The second view, then, is probably correct." Grounds: the πρός phrase's object is articular while the εἰς objects are anarthrous (not parallel); καταρτισμός is a verbal noun easily modified; context (vv. 7, 16) emphasizes "each one"/"each single part"; v.15 has all believers speaking truth. The "recent-egalitarian-innovation" charge (Lincoln, Gordon, Muddiman raise it) "would be difficult to make stick" — De Wette, Robinson, Westcott held it (Westcott himself a bishop). *Thielman siding with View 2.*
- **[4:12]** καταρτισμός (katartismos) — rare noun; medical sense = "setting" a joint/bone; nonliterary = "outfitting"/"equipping"/"preparation." Thielman: Paul's sense is "equipping"/"preparation," not "perfecting." *Thielman.*
- **[4:12]** Goal: οἰκοδομὴ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (building up the body of Christ) — recalls 2:20–22 architectural imagery, but now "evangelists, pastors, and teachers" added to apostles/prophets; metaphor "suddenly becomes organic" (building → body/church, 1:22–23). *Thielman.*
- **[4:13]** μέχρι καταντήσωμεν οἱ πάντες (until we all arrive; katantaō = arrive) attaches to the verbal idea in οἰκοδομήν, not to ἔδωκεν (pace Hoehner) — i.e., not "Christ keeps giving officers until we arrive" but "the building up continues until we arrive." Article οἱ with πάντες stresses that the whole is made of individuals (Robinson). *Thielman vs. Hoehner.*
- **[4:13]** Three parallel εἰς phrases viewing one result from different angles: (1) "unity [ἑνότητα] of the faith and of the knowledge [ἐπίγνωσις] of the Son of God" — faith = body of doctrine (the "one faith" of 4:5); ἐπίγνωσις = personal, experiential knowledge (cf. 1:17). (2) ἄνδρα τέλειον (mature man) — refers to the church, not the individual (as with 2:15, 21); note ἀνήρ ("adult male") vs. ἄνθρωπος of 2:15, contrasting maturity with the νήπιοι of v.14, possibly anticipating 5:29–32. (3) μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ — probably "height"/"stature" (Alford, Ellicott) rather than mature age; the church attains "Christ's full height." *Thielman.*

### 4:14–16 (growth into the head)

- **[4:14]** νήπιοι (infants) contrast the ἀνήρ τέλειος; immaturity's traits: ignorance, gullibility, individualism. Metaphor shifts to a storm at sea — "wave-tossed [κλυδωνιζόμενοι] and blown around by every wind [ἀνέμῳ] of teaching." *Thielman.*
- **[4:14]** κυβεία (kybeia) = lit. "dice-playing," hence cheating/deceit (Epictetus of philosophical fakes); τῶν ἀνθρώπων adjectival + negative — deception "merely 'human.'" Thielman links to the Colossian "philosophy" (Col 2:8). *Thielman.*
- **[4:14]** πανουργία (panourgia, cunning) — Paul's term for those falsifying God's word (2 Cor 4:2) and Satan's deception of Eve (2 Cor 11:3). *Thielman.*
- **[4:14]** μεθοδεία τῆς πλάνης (system of error) — μεθοδεία rare (only here + 6:11 in extant Greek to that point); Thielman argues it is NOT inherently sinister (later Ptolemy uses it for a mathematical "method"; Philo uses cognate neutrally) — it contributes "the idea of an intentional, organized approach." The sinister note comes from τῆς πλάνης (planned deception / doctrinal error). Paul probably links this "one great, erroneous plan" to "the Ruler of the realm of the air" (2:2; 6:11). *Thielman.*
- **[4:15]** ἀληθεύοντες (alētheuontes) — participle of means; "does not simply mean 'cherishing the truth'... but refers specifically to speaking the truth" — the gospel truth (cf. Gal 4:16; Eph 1:13). Manner "in love" (ἐν ἀγάπῃ) contrasts the false teaching's "trickery" and "cunning." *Thielman vs. Ellicott/Abbott/Robinson.*
- **[4:15]** "grow up to him" (αὐξήσωμεν εἰς αὐτόν) — organic, back to arriving "at a mature man" and the "growing temple" of 2:21; moving toward "full union with Christ." *Thielman.*
- **[4:15] kephalē** — Paul adds Christ is "the head" (κεφαλή) "perhaps to prevent the conclusion that the church is moving toward a union with Christ in which the distinction between the church and Christ is dissolved." Thielman: believers are NOT "growing 'into the head'" (pace Muddiman) but "growing 'up to Christ'... but Christ... is still the head of his body, the church." (See kephalē section below.) *Thielman vs. Muddiman.*
- **[4:16]** Christ as "the head" is "the source of the church's 'bodily' growth" — ἐξ οὗ (from whom); the head as "the control center of the body's growth," corresponding to "at least some ancient physiological thinking about the function of the brain" (Lloyd, Dawes; pace Bedale). Christ "produces" (ποιεῖται) the growth "for its own edification [οἰκοδομήν]." *Thielman.*
- **[4:16]** Body "being joined [συναρμολογούμενον] and held together [συμβιβαζόμενον]" — συναρμολογούμενον repeats 2:21; συμβιβάζω = "hold together" (as Col 2:19) but more often political "reconcile" warring parties — Paul "may have intended... those overtones." *Thielman.*
- **[4:16]** ἁφή (haphē, "connection/joint") — "unclear," core idea "touch or contact," here anatomical; medical dictionary glosses the plural as "ties." Too specific to render "ligaments/tendons"; means "any of the body's lines of connection." These provide ἐπιχορηγία (epichorēgia, "assistance/supply"). *Thielman.*
- **[4:16]** KEY: the "connections" are NOT a special class corresponding to the five gifted groups of v.11 (pace Lincoln, Schnackenburg, Muddiman). "every connection" = "each single part" (κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν ἐν μέτρῳ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου μέρους), echoing 4:7 — grace measured "to each Christian." Confirms Thielman's whole-body / all-believers reading of the section. *Thielman vs. Lincoln/Schnackenburg/Muddiman.*

## The descent (4:9) — Thielman's argument and the alternatives

Paul's rhetorical question: "he ascended" means "except that he also descended... εἰς τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς (eis ta katōtera tēs gēs, to the lower regions of the earth)." Thielman: "what was obvious to Paul... is no longer so clear." He canvasses the options:

**Option A — descent = the Spirit at Pentecost.** Christ ascends then descends in the Spirit; would fit Acts 2:33 and 4:11 gift-giving (W. H. Harris; cf. Abbott, Lincoln). **Thielman rejects** on two grounds: (1) in Acts 2 Christ sends the Spirit to all believers, but in 4:11 he sends "certain gifted individuals"; (2) 4:10 stresses the very same person (αὐτός) descended and ascended, yet in Ephesians "the work of Christ and the work of the Spirit are kept separate."

**Option B — descent = the incarnation (descent from heaven to earth first).** Supported by the early witnesses adding πρῶτον ("first") after κατέβη; fits Christ's pre-existence (1:4; 1 Cor 8:6), the Phil 2:6–8 / 2 Cor 8:9 pattern, and the Johannine ascent-as-return (John 3:13 etc.) — "the most common way in which early Christians spoke of the 'ascent' and 'descent.'" **Calvin's view** (1558 sermon): "Many have made glosses much too strong on this passage... a place forged out of their own brain" — Calvin took τῆς γῆς appositionally ("the lower regions, that is, the earth") = incarnation. By 1883 Eadie called this "the majority of expositors"; Schnackenburg said the old descensus reading was "now... abandoned." Problems this "newer approach" solves: Christ ascends from earth not under it; Ephesians has a two-tiered not three-tiered cosmos; the enemy powers are in the heavens, defeated at ascension. **Thielman rejects** it as probably misconstruing the grammar: "τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς is an odd way of referring to the surface of the earth" — Paul would have written εἰς τὰ κατώτερα or εἰς τὴν γῆν. "The most natural way to take the Greek... is as a reference to subterranean regions" (Muddiman).

**Option C — descent = to Hades / the realm of the dead (partitive/possessive genitive, "the earth's lower regions").** The pre-19th-c. consensus. Patristic/medieval purposes proposed: let OT saints become Christians (Tertullian, Jerome); give the dead a chance to hear the gospel (Ambrosiaster); rescue saints from limbo (Aquinas); or simply that Christ as human experienced death (Theodoret, Westcott, Büchsel, Masson, Hoehner, Gombis).

**Thielman's own position = a refined Option C.** He argues the cultural context (Greco-Roman underworld descents — Dionysus, Aeneas, Orpheus, Pythagoras; the Persephone myth on Asia-Minor coinage; the κατά/κατάγω/καταβαίνω vocabulary for going "down" to the dead) makes it "extremely unlikely" Paul meant anything but "a descent to the realm of the dead." BUT crucially he relocates the timing: the descent is **not** a journey between death and resurrection. Rather, "Christ's descent to the realm of the dead [is] not... something that happened between his death and resurrection, but... part of a single, triumphant event that included his ascent. After his resurrection, Christ both descended into the regions of the dead and ascended to a position above all the heavens." As with Ps 139:8 (cf. Jer 23:24; Jon 2; Rom 10:6–7), the descent-below / ascent-above pair "is a way of emphasizing the reach" of Christ "to every corner of the universe" — its purpose being "the defeat and captivity of all the malevolent powers of the universe" (v.8). Paul is "not concerned with geography but with the common association... between the realm of the dead and the fear" of the evils harbored there (Hades as torment/decay; imprisoned rebellious angels, 1 En. 10.12; 15.8–10; Jude 6; 2 Pet 2:4). All such powers are "now conquered" beneath Christ's feet (1:22); cf. Phil 2:10 (heavenly/earthly/subterranean) and 1 Pet 3:19–22.

**Textual note (Additional Note 4:9):** πρῶτον after κατέβη (witnesses אi2, B, C3, Ψ, Byz) would clarify descent-came-first (favoring incarnation), but the ancient/diverse witnesses omitting it (𝔓46, א*, A, C*, D, F, G...) make it "virtually certain" it was not original. Also μέρη after κατώτερα is "more evenly divided"; Thielman judges a scribe more likely to add than omit it.

## The "pastors and teachers" one-or-two-office question (4:11)

The fourth/fifth gifts share a single τοὺς δέ and are joined by καί (τοὺς δὲ ποιμένας καὶ διδασκάλους), occasioning two debates:

1. **Why grouped?** Some earlier commentators (Chrysostom, Theodoret, Ellicott, Abbott, Robinson): because pastors and teachers were "attached to a local congregation" while apostles/prophets/evangelists traveled. Thielman qualifies: "Not all apostles and prophets... conducted itinerant ministries" (James stayed in Jerusalem; the Corinthian prophets). He suggests instead the pairing may reflect a shared concern to guard against false teaching (4:14).

2. **One office or two?** Some (Alford, Eadie, Barth) take the single το὿ς δέ to mean pastors and teachers "were the same people with two sets of skills." **Thielman disagrees:** "The common τοὺς δέ, however, does not require this interpretation" — Paul used one article for "apostles" and "prophets" in 2:20 yet treated them as separate groups (Best, Hoehner). His conclusion: "Paul may have intended to imply that 'pastors' and 'teachers' were overlapping although not entirely identical groups," or the τοὺς δέ was simply "dropped as unnecessarily tedious repetition" (Muddiman). Bottom line: "the evidence is not clear enough to allow us to consider 'pastors' and 'teachers' as a single group." So Thielman: **overlapping but distinguishable, not simply one office.**

**Additional Note 4:11** treats two grammatical points: (a) Schnackenburg's claim that μὲν...δὲ...δέ contrasts apostles against the rest — Thielman rejects (the construction is "a normal way of listing discrete items," per Justin Dial. 39.2); (b) whether the articles are attributive ("the apostles, the prophets...") or pronominal ("some to be apostles, others to be prophets..."). Thielman favors the pronominal/predicate reading (BDAG, Muddiman, Hoehner) for two reasons: it supplies the otherwise-missing indirect object of ἔδωκεν, and the context emphasizes activities over offices — reinforcing his View-2 reading of v.12.

## kephalē (head) Christology (4:15–16)

- **[4:15]** Christ named "the head" (κεφαλή; cf. 1:22; 5:23; Col 1:18; 2:19) precisely to preserve the church/Christ distinction against a union "in which the distinction... is dissolved." Believers grow "up to Christ," **not** "into the head" (Thielman explicitly rejects Muddiman's "growing into the head").
- **[4:16]** As head, Christ is the **source** of bodily growth (ἐξ οὗ, "from whom"). Thielman reads kephalē here with a physiological nuance: "the head of the body as the control center of the body's growth, a concept that would correspond to at least some ancient physiological thinking about the function of the brain" (citing Lloyd 1973; Dawes 1998; explicitly "pace Bedale 1956" — i.e., against Bedale's influential "head = source/origin, not ruler" thesis). Thus kephalē carries both source-of-growth and directive/control-center connotations, and (via 1:22) headship as rule over the body. The head "produces" (ποιεῖται) the body's growth "for its own edification," and does so "in love" (ἐν ἀγάπῃ).

- synarmologoumenon / symbibazomenon (συναρμολογούμενον / συμβιβαζόμενον) — joined / held together (4:16)
- haphē (ἁφή) — connection/joint; epichorēgia (ἐπιχορηγία) — assistance/supply (4:16)

## Overflow (beyond assigned scope — §IX, lines 421–605)
Lines 421–605 open §IX "A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)": the section overview (4:17 as a rhetorical return to 4:1–3 after the "digressions" of 4:4–6 and 4:7–16); the two-part division of 4:17–24 (no-longer-walk-as-Gentiles + reminder of traditional ethical instruction, the clothing-change and old/new-human-being metaphors, "new human being... created after the pattern of God," κατὰ θεὸν κτισθείς, allusion to Gen 1:26); the seven exhortations of 4:25–5:2 (lying, anger, stealing, unedifying speech, grieving the Spirit, abusive speech, sacrificial love 5:1–2); and debate over whether 5:1–2 opens a new division, concludes the preceding, or (Thielman's preference) rounds the ethical advice back to imitation of God. This should be extracted by the slice covering 4:17ff., not folded into the 4:1–16 pages.
